questions.q: AdaGrad was built for rare features. Why not use it?
questions.a: Its denominator sums every past squared gradient, so each weight's rate only falls; the ADADELTA paper notes it heads to zero, and large early gradients keep it low for good. Google's click model used its own per-coordinate rate, close to AdaGrad's (our description), on a simpler, linear model.

teach.title: How it works: three generations of per-weight steps

questions.q: An embedding row gets no gradient this step. Does plain Adam leave it alone?
questions.a: An embedding is one learned vector per ID. In standard Adam a zero gradient still updates m and v, so the row keeps drifting on old momentum (our reading of the update rule). PyTorch 2.15's SparseAdam “only updates the moments and parameters corresponding to the non-zero values of the gradients”.

teach.title: How it works: three generations of per-weight steps

questions.q: Adam ignores gradient scale. So input scaling no longer matters?
questions.a: Kingma and Ba show that multiplying every gradient by a constant cancels out of Adam's step. Our reasoning: badly scaled inputs still make a lopsided loss surface, so standardising them is still cheap insurance.

teach.title: How it works: three generations of per-weight steps

questions.q: One weight's gradients are 2,000 times bigger than another's. Why does a single learning rate fail?
questions.a: Set it safe for the big one and the small one moves 2,000 times less; set it for the small one and the big one overshoots.

teach.title: How it works: three generations of per-weight steps

questions.q: What is AdaGrad's weakness, and how does RMSProp fix it?
questions.a: AdaGrad divides by the root of the sum of all past squared gradients, which only grows, so steps shrink towards zero. RMSProp uses a running average, which forgets old gradients.

questions.q: In Adam, a weight's gradient keeps flipping between +40 and −40. Big step or small?
questions.a: Small. Momentum cancels to about ±2.1 while √v is about 40, so the step is roughly the learning rate ÷ 20. Adam treats a flipping sign as noise.
